Movement I · Introduction and exposition

Allegro energico
E minor

Movement I (introduction and exposition) · Andante, ma non troppo – Allegro energico · E minor

994quarter-note beats51phrases175bars
12345678T

The home key is E minor. The introduction (mm.1–28) is a clarinet solo, and the exposition, Allegro energico, begins at m.29. The exposition runs to m.172 and moves through the first group, the transition, the restatement of the theme by the full orchestra, the second group and the closing group, in that order. I read the three bars from m.173 (rehearsal I) as the start of the development. The source breaks off in the third of these bars, so this reading was made without seeing what follows.

Nowhere in mm.1–175 are the tonic and the dominant connected in root position. The B major triad of m.170, which closes the exposition, is also the first dominant of E minor to sound in root position in the movement. In the tonal contexts assigned to the beats, E minor accounts for 297 beats (30%) and contexts with B as the tonic for 530 beats (53%). The E minor count includes the beats where the G–B sonority is read as the III region. A root-position E minor triad sounds on only 26 of the 994 beats.

These 26 beats make up four arrivals, at mm.37, 41, 83 and 87, and all four are entered from the sonority of III without a dominant. I read the E minor triads of mm.37 and 41 not as authentic cadences but as arrivals brought about by the theme's line. That line lies in the cellos' D3–E3 in mm.36 and 40, and the E minor triad sounds a beat early, on beat 6. These anticipating beats are also counted among the 26. The dominant of m.42, in which the leading tone D♯ first sounds, loses its root B over a G pedal before it resolves to the tonic in inversion.

The long F♯ of the second group is read as the dominant of B. In the 411 beats from m.97 beat 4, where the F♯ major triad enters, to m.165, the tonic B never once appears in the bass. The second half of the second group has only two chords, V7 and i6/4, and the interval at which they alternate shrinks at mm.150, 158 and 162. A cresc. molto runs on from m.162, but the resolution at m.166 is B in octaves, mf. The third, D♯, and the f come together four bars later, at m.170, where the exposition closes on this dominant of E minor without returning to the tonic.

1INT

mm.1–28

Introduction: the solo clarinet over the dominant B finds its way to G3

In mm.1–16 the timpani sustain B2 in a roll, and over it the clarinet plays alone. No chord ever sounds and the leading tone D♯ does not appear, but I read this B2 as the dominant pedal of E minor. The melody, now unaccompanied, arrives on the tonic E4 at m.20. In mm.22–28 the music of mm.2–8 returns exactly, a major sixth lower, and ends on G3. The clarinet re-attacks this G3 at m.29, and the Allegro begins over it.

INT1Paragraph 1: The clarinet's melody over the timpani's B2

Tonal contextE minor: dominant pedal B (can also be read as centered on B)

INT1a

B4 decorated by semitone neighbor notes (first half of K1)

m.1, beat 1 to m.5, beat 1E minor: dominant pedal B (can also be read as centered on B)

The clarinet enters on B4, the fifth degree of E minor, doubling the timpani's B2. In m.2, A♯4 a semitone below and C5 a semitone above decorate B4. D♯ does not sound, so if B is heard as the center, A♯ is the leading tone and C the Phrygian second degree. In m.4, A♯4 does not return to B4 but falls through A4 to the G4 of m.5.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.1, beat 1) ↓

INT1b

G4 decorated, then down to the tonic E4 (second half of K1)

m.5, beat 1 to m.9, beat 1E minor: from the fifth degree to the tonic over the dominant B

In mm.5–6 the shape of mm.1–2 is repeated on G4, with the neighbor notes F♯4 and A4 decorating G4. In m.7 G4 falls to F♯4, moving from a sixth to a fifth above the pedal B. The melody reaches the tonic E4 at m.8 beat 4, and the timpani reach mf in this bar. E4 moves on under the slur to the D4 of m.9, so there is no cadence.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.5, beat 1) ↓

INT1c

Rising to G4, with the pickup B3 in between (K2)

m.9, beat 1 to m.12, beat 4&E minor: dominant pedal B; B–D gives the sound of v

Each bar consists of a dotted half note and a pickup B3 at beat 4&. The dotted half notes rise D4–E4–F♯4–G4, moving the unit of m.9 up a major second, a major third and a perfect fourth. The pickup B3 has the same note name as the pedal and does not move. This ascent retraces the descent of mm.7–9 in reverse. While the clarinet makes a cresc., the timpani go into a dim.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.9, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 1The only third heard over the dominant B is the minor third, D
FINDING 1

The only third heard over the dominant B is the minor third, D

In the introduction the only third that sounds over the B2 pedal is D4 (mm.9, 13 and 14). No dominant chord containing the leading tone is ever formed over B. Before m.42 the only note to sound at the pitch of D♯ is the E♭4 of m.22.

INT1d

Down to B3 and the fermata (K3)

m.12, beat 4& to m.17, beat 1E minor: to the fifth degree B over the dominant pedal B (the tonic, if B is the center)

Melody K3 descends F♯4–E4–D4 and changes direction with the triplet C♯4–D4–E4 in m.14. C♯4 is the raised sixth degree and a neighbor note below D4. The melody drops a fourth from E4 to B3 and stays there for two bars, p morendo. B3 doubles the timpani's B2, and the melody settles on the same note as the pedal. With the fermata on the barline, the roll ends too.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.12, beat 4&) ↓

INT2Paragraph 2: The unaccompanied melody, and the opening melody returning a major sixth lower

Tonal contextE minor (tonic E4 at m.20) → G-minor implication

INT2a

From an arpeggiated iv to the tonic E4 (K4)

m.17, beat 1 to m.21, beat 1E minor: from an arpeggiated iv to the tonic E4

The unaccompanied clarinet rises through the A minor triad (iv) as an arpeggio. D4 is a passing note, and B4 a neighbor note above A4. B4–A4–G4–F♯4–E4 is the descent of mm.4–8 at the same pitch, without A♯4 and compressed into two bars. A rest follows the E4 at m.20 beat 3. This is the only place where a phrase of the introduction ends on the tonic of E minor.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.17, beat 1) ↓

INT2b

The first half of the opening melody a major sixth lower (K1′)

m.21, beat 1 to m.25, beat 1G-minor implication: the fifth degree D decorated by neighbor notes

The music of mm.22–24 is that of mm.2–4 transposed down nine semitones. The rest and the B4 of m.1 become a D4 lasting the whole bar in m.21. The neighbor notes C♯4 and E♭4 decorate D4, and the C♯4 of m.24 turns into a passing note to C4. The leading tone of G minor, F♯, does not sound, and the key is indicated only by the scale degrees of the melody.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.21, beat 1) ↓

INT2c

Arrival on the tonic G3, and on to the Allegro (K1′)

m.25, beat 1 to m.29, beat 1G-minor implication: from the third degree B♭ to the tonic G3

In mm.25–28 the music of mm.5–8 is transposed down nine semitones, and the neighbor notes A3 and C4 decorate B♭3. The melody arrives on the tonic G3 at m.28 beat 4. After the double bar, G3 is re-attacked at m.29 beat 1 and held until m.32 beat 1. The Allegro energico begins over this G3, and the B5 of Violins II replaces B♭ with B♮.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.25, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 2From the introduction to the transition, the key moves up a minor third again and again
FINDING 2

From the introduction to the transition, the key moves up a minor third again and again

In mm.25–28 the introduction's melody moves a major sixth below mm.5–8 and arrives on G3 instead of E4. The first group rises a minor third, from E minor to G major, and so does the transition, from B minor to D minor and to D (mm.52 and 69). At rehearsal D, conversely, the roots fall by minor thirds: C, A, F♯.

2MAIN

mm.29–48

First group: arrives in E minor without a dominant and closes in G major

Violins II hold the third G–B in tremolo, and from m.33 Violins I play the theme. The E minor triad is reached in root position at mm.37 and 41, but both times it is entered from the sonority of III without a dominant. The tutti dominant of m.42, in which the leading tone D♯ first sounds, resolves to i6 over the pedal G2. With G2 still unmoved, the G major triad becomes the tonic at m.47.

MAIN1Paragraph 1: The G–B tremolo, theme M and its repeat

Tonal contextFrom G–B (III) to root-position i (mm.37 and 41)

MAIN1a

The tremolo begins over the clarinet's G3

m.29, beat 1 to m.33, beat 1The third G–B (III; can also be read as i without its root)

The clarinet re-attacks G3, the last note of the introduction, making it the first bass of the Allegro. Above it Violins II repeat G5/B5 in eighth notes and from m.29 beat 4 sustain the dyad in tremolo. Only G and B sound: neither D, the fifth of the G major triad, nor E, the root of the E minor triad, has appeared yet. When the clarinet stops at m.32 beat 2, the tremolo alone remains for five beats.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.29, beat 1) ↓

MAIN1b

Theme M and the III–i arrival without a dominant

m.33, beat 1 to m.38, beat 1III (G–B) to i (m.37, without a dominant)

The G of the theme's head is held for nine beats and moves only with M1 in the second half of m.34. With the triplet at m.35 beat 1, E sounds for the first time in the Allegro, and the harmony becomes i6. In m.36 the violas and cellos trace the G–F♯–D–E of Violins I, playing the notes from F♯ onward in quarter notes. In the cellos this line becomes the bass, rising from the subtonic D3 to E3. The E minor triad of m.37 is a III–i arrival that does not pass through the leading tone D♯.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.33, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 3Only in the first group does the theme's line become the bass and lead to i
FINDING 3

Only in the first group does the theme's line become the bass and lead to i

In mm.36 and 40 the cellos play the theme's line G–F♯–D–E in the bass, rising from D3 to E3 to lead to i. In the restatement, at mm.82 and 86, this line lies above the timpani's G2. To reach the i of mm.83 and 87, the bass leaps a third, from G2 to E2.

MAIN1c

Repeat of mm.34–37 and the second i

m.38, beat 1 to m.42, beat 1III (G–B) to i again (m.41)

Every part repeats mm.34–37 at the same pitch and in the same rhythm. The G of the theme's head is not played anew: the G that was the third of i in m.37 simply continues. Only the dynamics differ, with the violas entering f at m.38 beat 4. At m.41 the music again arrives on the E minor triad without a dominant. The leading tone D♯ first sounds in the tutti of the next bar, m.42.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.38, beat 1) ↓

MAIN2Paragraph 2: The tutti turns to G major over the G pedal

Tonal contextE minor (over the G pedal) → G major (III)

MAIN2a

The dominant resolves to i6 over the G pedal

m.42, beat 1 to m.45, beat 1E minor: V♭9 → i6 (over the G pedal)

With the tutti at m.42 beat 2, a dominant containing the leading tone sounds for the first time. The chord is V♭9, with C added, and the bass remains G2. On beat 6 the root B falls to A, and the sonority becomes the diminished seventh on the leading tone, D♯–F♯–A–C. In m.43 every voice moves by step and resolves to i6. Figure U in m.44 arpeggiates the tonic and resolves the leading tone D♯ to the tonic E.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.42, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 4The dominant of E minor loses its root B before it resolves to the tonic
FINDING 4

The dominant of E minor loses its root B before it resolves to the tonic

At m.42 beat 2 the tutti sounds B–D♯–F♯–C over G2, bringing C and D♯ into the Allegro for the first time. On beat 6 every B drops to A, and the diminished seventh on the leading tone resolves to i6. At m.88, too, the dominant loses its root before it moves to the tonic.

MAIN2b

Through Am7/G and D7/G to G major

m.45, beat 1 to m.49, beat 1E minor → G major: iv4/2 – V7 – I

The G2 pedal continues and now becomes the seventh of Am7. This chord is iv4/2 of E minor and at the same time ii4/2 of G major. Figure U in m.46 arpeggiates Am7, and on beat 4 the chord changes to D7/G. V7 resolves to I over the bass G, and at m.47 the music arrives in G major. The chord is held by ties until m.48 beat 4, and only the repeated notes of the lower strings last to the end of the bar.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.45, beat 1) ↓

3TRAN

mm.49–78

Transition: from B minor through a sequence and the wedge to the dominant seventh of G major

At rehearsal A the woodwinds play a new motive in B minor and repeat it a minor third higher, in D minor. The strings head for A minor and, repeating this a whole tone higher, arrive in B minor (mm.55–63). At m.67 the harmony of the B minor figure changes to D7/A. From m.70 the outer voices open out chromatically in a wedge on either side of the pedal D. Rehearsal B presents four chords in succession, but only D7/A functions as the dominant of G major.

TRAN1Paragraph 1: Motive W in B minor and D minor (rehearsal A)

Tonal contextB minor (v) → D minor, a minor third higher

TRAN1a

Motive W in B minor (rehearsal A)

m.49, beat 1 to m.52, beat 1B minor: i6/4 → i (timpani B2)

Motive W is three bars long: an F♯ tied over five beats followed by a quarter-note F♯, a neighbor-note figure in the rhythm of figure U, and a single closing stroke. For the first three beats the bassoons' F♯3 is the lowest note, giving i6/4, and from beat 4 the timpani's B2 supports the root. At m.51 beat 4 the motive falls from F♯ to B and closes with a two-beat rest.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.49, beat 1) ↓

TRAN1b

Motive W repeated a minor third higher, in D minor

m.52, beat 1 to m.54, beat 4D minor: i6/4 → i (timpani D3)

The oboes, horns and timpani (D3, più f) transpose mm.49–51 exactly up a minor third. The flutes and clarinets join, and the bassoons add the lower octave. Their A2–B♭2–A2–G2 lies below the timpani's D3 and is the lowest note beat by beat. Even so, D3 is taken as a pedal, and the passage is read with the same functions as mm.49–51. The closing stroke at m.54 beat 4 coincides with the strings' pickup.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.52, beat 1) ↓

TRAN2Paragraph 2: The string phrase, the model of the sequence

Tonal contextA minor: VII–IV7–V7–V7♭9 (→ i)

TRAN2a

The string phrase: G–D7/A–E7/B–E7♭9

m.54, beat 4 to m.59, beat 1A minor: VII–IV7–V7–V7♭9 (→ i)

Violins I and the cellos take over the rhythm of motive W in the strings. The bass rises G2–A2–B2, and the melody's D5 changes its role from fifth to root to seventh. The C♯–D oscillation of m.56 is figure N, with C♯ as the lower neighbor note of the root D. In m.58 the harmony becomes E7♭9 over the E3 of Horns III–IV, and from beat 4 E2 supports the root. The chord resolves to the A minor triad at m.59, and the sequence a whole tone higher begins.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.54, beat 4) ↓

FINDING 5The I–V4/3 of G major veers toward A minor over the bass B2
FINDING 5

The I–V4/3 of G major veers toward A minor over the bass B2

The G major triad and D7/A of mm.55–56 sound as I–V4/3 over the bass G2–A2. Over the B2 of m.57, however, it is E7/B, not I6, that sounds, and the music turns toward A minor. The passage a whole tone higher, mm.59–61, does the same, but the third stage, mm.63–64, stays on the B minor triad.

TRAN3Paragraph 3: Sequence a whole tone higher, to B minor

Tonal contextA minor → B minor (sequence a whole tone higher)

TRAN3a

Second stage of the sequence: from A minor to F♯7♭9

m.59, beat 1 to m.63, beat 1A minor: i → B minor: IV7–V7–V7♭9 (→ i)

This stage is the string phrase of mm.55–58 moved up a whole tone. The A minor triad of m.59 resolves the E7♭9 of the previous bar and is at the same time the first chord of the B-minor stage. Raising the model's VII by a whole tone would give an A major triad, but the horns and inner voices sound C♮, not C♯. The music of mm.60–62 is an exact transposition of the model, and the melody's E5 changes its role from fifth to root to seventh. At m.63 F♯7♭9 resolves to the B minor triad.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.59, beat 1) ↓

Tonal contextB minor (v) → D (III of B minor, V of G major)

The woodwinds sound the rhythm of motive W in B minor

The F♯7♭9 of m.62 resolves to the B minor triad, and B minor lasts for four bars. TRAN4b

The same figure over D7/A, arriving on D

m.67, beat 1 to m.70, beat 1D: III7 in 4/3 position → III (V of G major)

The woodwind figure of mm.63–65 is reharmonized while its upper voice keeps F♯5. The bass falls from B1 to A1, and the oboes, bassoons and horns add the seventh, C♮. First half of the wedge: the bass from D3 to G2

m.70, beat 1 to m.73, beat 1Chromatic: contrary motion in the outer voices over the D pedal

From m.70 beat 6 the horns re-attack D3/D4 every two beats and, together with the timpani's D3, form an inner pedal. At m.72 beat 6 a G major triad sounds in root position.

FINDING 6

The wedge's bass does not stop at the G major triad on G2 but descends to G1

At m.72 beat 6 a G major triad sounds in root position over G2. From there the bass descends by semitones, and at rehearsal B the bass at the start of each bar is C2, B1, B♭1 and A1 in turn. At the same points the top voice rises from E♭6 to F♯6, and the outer voices arrive on G1 and G6 at m.79.

TRAN6Paragraph 6: Rehearsal B, four chords with scales

Tonal contextA chain of roots on a whole-tone scale → V4/3 of G major

TRAN6a

A♭/C and E7/B, two chords with scales

m.74, beat 6 to m.77, beat 1A chain that establishes no key: A♭/C → E7/B

On beats 4–6 the brass rest, and only the ascending and descending scales sound. The scales use the notes of A♭ major in m.75 and of A major in m.76, and at the end of each bar they return to the highest and lowest notes of that bar. At beat 6 + 3/4 the brass anticipate the next chord with a sixteenth note. The root moves from A♭ down a major third to E, and A♭4 remains as G♯4.

FINDING 7Two common tones link the four chords of rehearsal B
FINDING 7

Two common tones link the four chords of rehearsal B

Rehearsal B moves through A♭/C, E7/B, B♭7 and D7/A. The trumpets' A♭4 (G♯4 in m.76) is the root, the third and the seventh of the first three chords. The D4 in the brass is the seventh, the third and the root of the last three, and the two notes form the tritone common to E7 and B♭7.

TRAN6b

From B♭7 to V4/3 of G major (D7/A)

m.77, beat 1 to m.79, beat 1B♭7 → V4/3 of G major

The root moves from E to B♭, a tritone away, and the chord shares the tritone D–G♯ (A♭) with E7. From beat 4 the timpani begin a roll on D3 and keep it up to the end of m.78. The D7/A of m.78 is V4/3 of G major, and here the chain has a key for the first time. The brass do not anticipate, and the outer notes of the scales, F♯6 and A1, proceed to the G6 and G1 of m.79.

4CS

mm.79–99

Restatement of the theme: the tutti does not close in G major but veers off to an F♯ major triad

At rehearsal C the tutti restates the theme an octave higher, ff. The E minor triad is again reached without a dominant, at mm.83 and 87. The dominant of m.88 likewise resolves to i6 over the pedal G1, but this time there is no turn to G major. At m.93 the bass moves to C, and fragments of the theme sound over C major and A minor triads. At m.97 beat 4 an F♯ major triad enters, fff.

CS3b

The theme's head and the fragments M1 and M2 over the A minor triad

m.96, beat 1 to m.97, beat 4E minor: iv → iv7

The trumpets take the theme's head. They lower the E held for nine beats since m.95 to D and then B, forming M1, and in m.97 they play M2 in triplets. M1 is the model transposed diatonically down a third, and M2 is the model moved down a major third. With G4 added the chord becomes iv7, and at the end of beat 3 everyone cuts off.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.96, beat 1) ↓

CS3c

The F♯ major triad and the four-voice canon on figure Z

m.97, beat 4 to m.100, beat 1V/V of E minor = V of B major (F♯7)

After the A minor triad, the F♯ major triad, which shares no common tone with it, enters fff. The timpani retuned from G to F♯ in m.93, and this F♯2 becomes the pedal of the second group. Each of the four voices of the canon plays a half-note F♯ followed by Z (E–B♯–C♯–F♯), entering every three beats an octave lower. E falls on beat 1 or beat 4, and each time the chord becomes F♯7. The last voice arrives on F♯2 at m.100 beat 1.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.97, beat 4) ↓

FINDING 9The top-voice E6 becomes the third, the fifth and the seventh of three chords
FINDING 9

The top-voice E6 becomes the third, the fifth and the seventh of three chords

The E6 at m.98 beat 1 is the seventh of F♯7. The same E6 had been in the top voice from m.93 to m.97 beat 3, as the third of the C major triad and the fifth of the A minor triad. E drops out only for the three beats of the F♯ major triad, which has no common tone with the A minor triad.

5SGA

mm.100–128

Second group (first half): B major over F♯ turns to B minor with a single G♮

The string ostinato alternates an F♯ major and a C♯ minor triad every three beats. The two chords are read as V and ii of B major, but the tonic B never appears in the bass. At rehearsal E the flutes play a theme in thirds, and the woodwinds answer. At m.121 beat 4 G♯ changes to G♮, and ii becomes iiø7 of B minor. At rehearsal F a pizzicato theme is set in canon over this C♯ø7.

SGA1Paragraph 1: The F♯ chord and the ostinato O

Tonal contextB major: V–ii6 (F♯ pedal partly implied)

SGA1a

Rhythm R over F♯ alternating with the ostinato O

m.100, beat 1 to m.104, beat 1B major: V (F♯) alternating with ii6

The second group begins with R over F♯. The strings' O alternates F♯–A♯–C♯ and E–G♯–C♯ every three beats, with Violins I holding C♯. There is no bass in mm.101 and 103, and in m.102 the trombones (pp) repeat the R of m.100. F♯ is taken as an implied pedal, and O is read as V–ii6 of B major.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.100, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 10The ostinato splits F♯9 into two triads
FINDING 10

The ostinato splits F♯9 into two triads

The only notes heard in mm.100–107 are the five pitches F♯, A♯, C♯, E and G♯. The ostinato divides this dominant ninth chord into two triads that share C♯. All five notes first sound together at m.107 beat 4, where the harp falls out of step.

SGA1b

The ostinato O alone continues, and the harp joins

m.104, beat 1 to m.108, beat 1B major: V–ii6 (F♯ pedal implied)

The same O as in m.103 continues for four bars. From m.105 the harp (p) joins, doubling the strings' chords in two octaves. In m.107 the harp's half notes fall out of step with the strings, and on beat 4 the two chords overlap. The phrase lasts until m.108 beat 1, where the flute theme enters at rehearsal E.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.104, beat 1) ↓

SGA2Paragraph 2: Rehearsal E, the flute theme S1 and its answer

Tonal contextB major: V–ii6 over F♯; the answer ii7–V–ii

SGA2a

The flutes' theme S1 in thirds

m.108, beat 1 to m.111, beat 6B major: V–ii6 alternation (F♯ pedal implied)

The two flutes play the staccato theme in two voices a third apart. The theme rises in m.108, and in mm.109–111 the first notes of the bars descend through the F♯ major triad, C♯6–A♯5–F♯5. After the triplet of m.111 the two voices descend by step and arrive on unison C♯5. The theme does not reach the tonic B but stops on the second degree, C♯. Beneath it the ostinato O has not changed since m.107, and there is no bass.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.108, beat 1) ↓

SGA2b

The answer S1r and its repeat an octave lower

m.111, beat 6 to m.115, beat 1B major: ii7–V–ii (over the F♯ pedal)

The answer moves from the pickup ii7 to V and, after Oboe I's octave leap, on to ii. The timpani strike the triplet figure TT on F♯2, and the low F♯ sounds for the first time since m.102. From m.113 beat 6 the clarinets and bassoons repeat the same answer an octave lower. Both answers close on the C♯m7 of beat 6. The flutes hold C♯5 until m.113.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.111, beat 6) ↓

SGA3Paragraph 3: Theme S1 doubled by the horns, and the turn to G♮

Tonal contextB major (bass F♯–C♯) → B minor (m.121)

SGA3a

Theme S1 doubled by the horns, and the F♯–C♯ bass

m.115, beat 1 to m.118, beat 6B major: V–ii alternation (bass F♯2–C♯3)

The flute theme and the ostinato O are the same as in mm.108–111. The horns double the theme an octave lower and leave out the triplet in m.118. The double basses play F♯2–C♯3–F♯2–C♯3 pizzicato, and the second chord of O becomes ii over its root. The C♯3 on beat 2 is an alternating bass note within V.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.115, beat 1) ↓

SGA3b

The answer restated, and the turn to B minor through G♮

m.118, beat 6 to m.123, beat 1B major → B minor (m.121 beat 4, G♮)

The answer from m.118 beat 6 is the same as the one from m.111 beat 6, with the flutes and horns holding C♯. In m.120 the music is the same as in m.113, but the second answer does not come. At m.121 beat 4 the G♯ of the ostinato O is replaced by G♮, and ii becomes iiø7 of B minor. The last answer runs iiø7–V7–iiø7. The fz chord at m.122 beat 6 is tied into rehearsal F.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.118, beat 6) ↓

FINDING 11The third of B major, D♯, sounds only in the melody
FINDING 11

The third of B major, D♯, sounds only in the melody

At m.121 beat 4 the ostinato's G♯ changes to G♮, and ii becomes iiø7. Of the ostinato's notes, this G♯ alone separates B major from B minor. Apart from grace notes, D♯ appears only in the theme S1, and after m.118 it does not sound again until m.170.

SGA4Paragraph 4: Rehearsal F, the pizzicato theme and the canon

Tonal contextB minor: from iiø7 to the alternation of V7 and iiø7 over F♯

SGA4a

The pizzicato theme and the canon a bar behind

m.123, beat 1 to m.127, beat 1B minor: iiø7 (C♯–E–G–B) prolonged

The violins' theme moves up and down in quarter notes, then descends F♯–E–D–C♯. The violas and cellos play the same melody a bar later, one and two octaves lower. In mm.125–126, a restatement of mm.123–124, the flutes add a voice a third below and then one a sixth below. The chord is C♯ø7 in all four bars, and the theme's non-chord tones are passing notes.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.123, beat 1) ↓

SGA4b

V7 and iiø7 alternate over F♯

m.127, beat 1 to m.128, beat 6B minor: V7 alternating with iiø7 (over the F♯ pedal)

The shape of mm.127 and 128 is almost the same: in each bar the first half is V7 and the second half iiø7 over F♯. The triplets of the timpani and flutes bring back the F♯ that had broken off. Only on beat 1 do the timpani rest, and there the double basses' C♯3 is the lowest note. The violins shorten the theme to E–F♯–E–C♯. The pickup at m.128 beat 6 belongs to the next phrase.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.127, beat 1) ↓

6SGB

mm.129–165

Second group (second half): over the F♯ pedal the alternation of V7 and i6/4 quickens

At the Tranquillo the flutes and clarinets answer the oboe's melody. From m.130 the double basses hold F♯1, the lowest note of the extract. Above it there are only two chords, V7 and i6/4 of B minor, and V7 does not move to i in root position but keeps changing places with i6/4. The interval between changes shrinks from three bars to two at m.150, to three or six beats at m.158 and to three beats at m.162.

SGB1Paragraph 1: The Tranquillo oboe melody and its answer

Tonal contextB minor: from V7 without its root to V7 and i6/4

SGB1a

The oboe holds the seventh of V7

m.128, beat 6 to m.133, beat 1B minor: from V7 without its root to V7 and i6/4

The oboe rises from D5 to E5 and holds the seventh of V7 for 15 beats. In m.129 the strings' chord lacks its root F♯; the double basses' F♯1 is added in m.130. In m.131 (poco ritenuto) the oboe moves E–D–E–C♯ and arrives on B4 at rehearsal G. As B4 sounds, the strings change to i6/4, but the bass F♯ does not move.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.128, beat 6) ↓

FINDING 12Even when the F♯ pedal breaks off, the bass does not go to B
FINDING 12

Even when the F♯ pedal breaks off, the bass does not go to B

At m.129 (Tranquillo) even the F♯ pedal breaks off, and C♯3 becomes the bass, as at rehearsal F. From m.97 beat 4 to m.165 there is no beat with B in the bass.

SGB1b

The answer in the flutes and clarinets

m.133, beat 1 to m.135, beat 1B minor: i6/4 (over the dominant pedal F♯)

The answer moves F♯–E–F♯–C♯ in the same rhythm as the oboe in m.131. Its first three notes lie a whole tone above the oboe's, but the fourth, C♯, is the same note, and it moves not to B but a semitone up to D. In m.134 the answer closes with a triplet neighbor note and then arrives on the C♯ of m.135. The chord remains i6/4 in both bars.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.133, beat 1) ↓

SGB2Paragraph 2: Melody and answer restated, hemiola

Tonal contextB minor: from V7 over the F♯ pedal to i6/4

SGB2a

The melody restated (shortened, with an insertion)

m.135, beat 1 to m.139, beat 1B minor: V7 (mm.135–137) to i6/4

This restates mm.129–132, but E5 shrinks to nine beats. In m.136 the melody ends E–D–E–B, and B appears early, outside the chord. A new bar is inserted at m.137, moving the figure of the answer in m.134 down a second. When the melody arrives on B4 in m.138, the strings change to the same i6/4 as in m.132. The strings' V7 contains no C♯, and the fifth is supplied by the winds alone.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.135, beat 1) ↓

SGB2b

The answer, with a hemiola

m.139, beat 1 to m.141, beat 1B minor: i6/4 (over the dominant pedal F♯)

This restates the answer of mm.132–135, and mm.138 and 141 have the same notes as the model. In m.139 the answer becomes four dotted quarters, F♯–E–F♯–G, forming a hemiola. In m.140 it holds F♯ in the rhythm of m.134 and closes with a triplet neighbor note. The answer arrives on the C♯ of m.141, where the oboe's third entry begins.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.139, beat 1) ↓

SGB3Paragraph 3: The melody's third statement and the bassoon countermelody

Tonal contextB minor: from V7 over the F♯ pedal to i6/4

SGB3a

The melody's third statement and the bassoon countermelody

m.141, beat 1 to m.145, beat 1B minor: V7 (mm.141–143) to i6/4

The oboe repeats mm.135–138 with the same notes and arrives on B4 in m.144. The bassoons repeat their figure of rising thirds a third higher, then descend D3–C♯3–B2–A♯2. As the oboe reaches B4, the bassoons too arrive on the tonic B2, from the leading tone A♯2. From m.143 the marking is Poco a poco più stretto e crescendo. In m.144 the strings change to i6/4, and their repeated notes are now aligned with the beat.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.141, beat 1) ↓

SGB3b

The answer cut to one bar, and the rising scale

m.145, beat 1 to m.146, beat 1B minor: i6/4 (over the dominant pedal F♯)

The answer is the same F♯–E–F♯–C♯ as in m.133, but it ends after one bar. Rehearsal H falls at m.146, the bar that corresponds to the answer's second bar, and there the flutes and clarinets enter on the same D as in m.134. The bassoons rise from B2 to F♯4 through the melodic minor scale of B minor. G♯ and A♯ are the sixth and seventh degrees raised for the ascent, and the chord does not change.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.145, beat 1) ↓

SGB4Paragraph 4: Rehearsal H, woodwind lines in contrary motion

Tonal contextB minor: i6/4 and V7 alternate over the F♯ pedal

SGB4a

Rehearsal H, two woodwind lines in contrary motion

m.146, beat 1 to m.150, beat 1B minor: i6/4 to V7 (mm.147–149)

The woodwinds divide into two lines, the flutes and clarinets playing the upper one and the bassoons the lower. From m.147 Oboe I joins the upper line and Oboe II the lower (mf). The two lines move mostly in contrary motion, exchanging two notes of the chord and linking them with a passing note. Over i6/4 they link B and D with C♯; over V7 they link C♯ and E with D. This i6/4 is the last of three bars that run from m.144, and mm.147–149 are V7.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.146, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 13From rehearsal H the woodwinds play the leading tone A♯ only as a grace note
FINDING 13

From rehearsal H the woodwinds play the leading tone A♯ only as a grace note

Apart from grace notes, the woodwinds in mm.146–165 play only B, C♯, D, E, F♯ and G. The leading tone A♯ is played by the strings, and the woodwinds' G is confined to the ♭9 of V7 on beat 5 of mm.152 and 156. In m.139 the same G5/G6 was a neighbor note over i6/4.

SGB4b

Two-bar alternation and the harp's F♯

m.150, beat 1 to m.154, beat 1B minor: i6/4 and V7 alternate every two bars

This is a variation of mm.146–149, with i6/4 and V7 now lasting two bars each. The upper line of m.151 is the same as in m.147, and the E on beat 1 and the C♯ on beat 3 become non-chord tones. In m.152 every part except the harp is marked fz, and the harp adds F♯. The G on beat 5 is the ♭9 of V7 and has the same grace note A as in m.139. The upper line of m.153 is the same as in m.149.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.150, beat 1) ↓

SGB4c

Repeat of mm.150–153

m.154, beat 1 to m.158, beat 1B minor: i6/4 and V7 alternate every two bars

This repeats mm.150–153, with the woodwinds, Violins II, the violas, the lower strings and the timpani sounding the same notes. In mm.154–155 the F♯5 of Violins I and the harp are added. The fz falls on beat 1 of mm.154 and 156. After the V7 of m.157, the alternation shrinks to half a bar from m.158.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.154, beat 1) ↓

SGB5Paragraph 5: Half-bar alternation and the dissolution of the figure

Tonal contextB minor: i6/4 and V7 alternate over the F♯ pedal

SGB5a

Half-bar alternation and the nine-beat unit

m.158, beat 1 to m.162, beat 1B minor: i6/4 and V7 over the F♯ pedal

The two-bar alternation of mm.150–157 shrinks here to half a bar. The woodwinds and strings take the nine beats i6/4–V7–i6/4 as a unit and play it three times. The start of each unit (m.158 beat 1, m.159 beat 4, m.161 beat 1) carries an fz. The last three beats of the third statement also serve as the first half of the one-bar pattern of the next phrase.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.158, beat 1) ↓

SGB5b

One bar four times, cresc. molto

m.162, beat 1 to m.166, beat 1B minor: i6/4→V7 four times, the last V7 going to I

The bar of m.162 is played four times in succession, through m.165. Its first half is the same as m.159 beats 1–3, its second half the same as m.158 beats 4–6. The rising B–C♯–D drops out of the woodwind lines, and only the neighbor notes around D and F♯ and the voice exchange of V7 remain. The i6/4 and V7 alternate every three beats. The V7 in the second half of m.165 is the last chord over the F♯ pedal.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.162, beat 1) ↓

7CLOS

mm.166–172

Closing group: the F♯ pedal resolves to B in octaves, and the third arrives late

At Tempo I, V7 resolves, mf, to B in octaves without a third. In the next three bars the pizzicato strings and the timpani play the same B in a low register, once in each bar. The B major triad that sounds f at m.170, with the third, D♯, added, is the tonic of B major and also the dominant of E minor. The closing figure descends through the strings and lands on B1 at m.173 beat 1.

CLOS1Paragraph 1: From B octaves to the B major triad

Tonal contextB: from I without its third to B major (V of E minor)

CLOS1a

Resolution of V7: B without its third

m.166, beat 1 to m.170, beat 1B: I without its third (major or minor undecided)

The V7 of m.165 resolves at Tempo I to B in octaves. What follows the cresc. molto is a single beat at mf, with the timpani's B2 as the lowest note. In mm.167–169 the strings (pizz.) and the timpani play the same stroke three times, spanning B1 to B3. In every bar beats 2–6 are rests. No third sounds, and whether B is major or minor remains undecided.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.166, beat 1) ↓

CLOS1b

The B major triad and the closing figure Q

m.170, beat 1 to m.173, beat 1B major: I (also V of E minor)

In m.170 D♯ is added, and the B major triad is held for three bars. Q descends from the tonic B to the sixth degree G♯, circles around G♯, then arpeggiates down through the tonic triad. At m.171 beat 4 the lower strings begin the same Q one and two octaves below Violins II and the violas. From beat 5 of that bar, Q becomes the lowest voice, moving beneath the held chord. The final B1/B2 of Q falls on m.173 beat 1 and begins the pedal that is read as the start of the development.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.170, beat 1) ↓

FINDING 14In the chord that closes the exposition, the dominant of E minor is complete in root position for the first time
FINDING 14

In the chord that closes the exposition, the dominant of E minor is complete in root position for the first time

At m.170 D♯ and an f are added to the B octaves (mf) of mm.166–169. This is the first time in the movement that B–D♯–F♯ sounds with B in the bass. The dominants of mm.42 and 88 both stood over a G pedal.

8DEV

mm.173–175

Start of the development: B1, the landing note of the closing figure, becomes a pedal

From rehearsal I the bassoons and double basses hold B1, the last note of the closing figure. The timpani keep striking B2. No triad sounds any more. At m.175 C♯2 is added and clashes with B1 at the interval of a second. The source breaks off here, so the reading of this block was made without seeing what follows.

DEV1Paragraph 1: Rehearsal I, the pedal B and C♯

Tonal contextB (no third); B–C♯, a second, at m.175

DEV1a

The pedal B and C♯ (end of the source)

m.173, beat 1 to end of m.175B (no third); C♯ added at m.175

B1, the last note of the closing figure Q, directly becomes the double basses' pedal. The triad and the upper voices vanish, and only the octave B1/B2 remains. At m.175 the bassoons and cellos add C♯2, which clashes with B1 at a second. Whether B is the dominant of E minor or the center of a key with B as its tonic cannot be decided from these three bars. The source breaks off at m.175 with the ties left open.

Beat-by-beat analysis (from m.173, beat 1) ↓

Every beat

Beat-by-beat analysis

Choose a bar range or a phrase to read a short stretch. Open “Sounding notes and bass” to check each reading against the sounding pitches of each instrument family.

How to read the table (positions, chord labels, functions)
  • All beats are counted in quarter notes: four to the bar in mm.1–28 (2/2) and six from m.29 on (6/4). The conductor's beats fall on beats 1 and 3 in 2/2 and on beats 1 and 4 in 6/4. The metronome mark of the Allegro energico, dotted half = 108, is in a different unit from the table's beats.
  • The exact halfway point of a beat is written “beat N&” in the prose and “+1/2” in chord labels. +1/4 and +3/4 are the positions that divide the beat into four, and +1/3 and +2/3 are triplet positions. Where a chord label has an arrow (→), the chord before the arrow sounds at the start of the beat, and the chord after it enters at the position written after it (“at +1/2”, for example).
  • All pitch names are sounding pitches. The clarinets in A, the horns and trumpets in F, and the double basses sound at a different pitch from the written one. When you compare the table with the full score, please read these parts transposed. The harp is written with a C♭ major key signature in mm.103–120, but the table spells its notes with sharps, in line with the other instruments.
  • The number after a pitch name is its octave number, with C4 as middle C. Two notes sounding together are written from the lower note up, as in “G3/B3”, but this is a different notation from the slash of a chord label.
  • The pitch name after a slash is the lowest note actually sounding at that moment, whichever instrument plays it. A chord over a pedal is written like “B minor/F♯”, and the Function column names the pedal. Even where an instrument doubling the melody in a low register goes below the pedal, the label follows the lowest note.
  • Every note a label names is sounding at that moment. In a label, “no3” and “no5” (no 3rd, no 5th) mean that the third or the fifth does not sound. Passing and neighbor notes in the melody are left out of the label and described in the Comment column. A non-chord tone that sounds with the chord through a whole beat, such as an appoggiatura, is kept in the label as “(add X)”.
  • Some beats have only a melody, or only two sounding notes. For these the label names only what sounds (“bare B”, “G–B major third” and the like). The harmonic meaning is given in the Function column, and where there is no basis for deciding a root, none is decided.
  • The home key of the movement is E minor. The Tonal context column gives the key that frames the reading of the beat; it does not mean that the music modulates from beat to beat.
  • Roman numerals refer to the tonal context given with them. Minor triads are written in lower case (i, iv), major triads in upper case (III, V). V/x is the secondary dominant of x. Inversions are shown with figures, as in i6 or V4/3. ø7 is a half-diminished seventh chord, °7 a diminished seventh chord.
  • Where another reading is realistic, the beat's comment, or the tonal context of the phrase or paragraph, says “can also be read as”. The confidence of each beat (high, medium, low) is not shown on the page but is kept in the analysis data.
  • Paragraphs and phrases are analytical groupings based on entries, rests, cadences and thematic repetition. A phrase's span is given by its start and end positions, and the beat at the end position is itself not included.
  • Each phrase's “Key chord progression” reduces the orchestral sound to a grand staff. It shows the actual lowest note and each note that the label names, and each note is written at one of the octaves in which it actually sounds. Notes that lie far outside the staff are moved by an octave.
  • The material tags used in the beat table and the text are as follows.

It can also be read as IV of G major, but since the cadence on G was avoided in mm.91–92, it is read as VI of E minor.

Phrase CS3a begins ↑ · m.93 beat 1. Rehearsal D. Over the double basses' C2 the woodwinds (f) begin to reiterate the C major triad in quarter notes, and the horns, violas and cellos sustain C.
